The service name governed by these Terms of Service is Airbnb.

Here's a plain-language summary:

**Key Provisions:**

* The Terms of Service apply to all products and services described on Airbnb's official terms page.
* When you use Airbnb, you grant the company permission to use your submitted content to improve and train their AI/ML systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* Airbnb collects personal data as outlined in their published Privacy Policy.
* In case of a dispute, you and Airbnb are required to use binding arbitration with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (unless you created your account before this opt-out window was introduced). This means you'll have to resolve disputes privately with Airbnb instead of going to court.
* Either party can terminate the agreement if the other party breaches the terms or if there's a material change that impacts the agreement.
* If you have questions, you can contact Airbnb through their published legal contact information.

**Potential Risks to Users:**

* Binding arbitration may limit your ability to participate in class-action lawsuits, potentially impacting the benefits of collective claims or settlements.
* Airbnb's use of user-submitted content to train their AI/ML systems may lead to unintended consequences or conflicts with users' interests.
* The Terms of Service do not provide a clear explanation of how your data will be handled, leaving some room for concern regarding data protection and handling.

**Other Important Notes:**

* Airbnb requires users to create an account, so registering an account implies acceptance of these terms.
* There's an opt-out window for users to bypass binding arbitration for new accounts, giving existing users some flexibility.
* While arbitration provisions are mandatory, it's good to know that Steam has removed mandatory arbitration for its service.

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — AIRBNB TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Airbnb and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added new AnyWhere/Icons experience terms, revised cancellation and refund policies (including AirCover updates), added language on automated/AI-driven listing detection (e.g. anti-party tools), and updated arbitration provisions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Airbnb to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2908 . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.airbnb.com/help/article/2908 .

**Scope**: These terms apply to your relationship with Cloudflare and govern the use of their products and services listed on their official terms page.

However, for accounts created within 30 days, you may opt-out of this requirement. Note that some companies might have changed their mandatory arbitration policies since Cloudflare's update.

**Contact**: If you have questions about these terms, you can find Cloudflare's contact information at their published URL.

source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — CLOUDFLARE SELF-SERVE SUBSCRIPTION AGREEMENT (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Cloudflare and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added AI Gateway and Workers AI specific terms, clarified that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare's models, and revised acceptable-use rules with stronger anti-scraping/AI-bot abuse language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Cloudflare to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.cloudflare.com/terms/ .

**Stripe Services Agreement (US)** is the set of rules that govern your relationship with Stripe, a payment processing service. These terms help ensure that both parties are clear about their responsibilities and rights.

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope:** The terms apply to the products and services listed on Stripe's official terms page.
* **Content and License:** Stripe uses your submitted content to improve and train its AI systems, subject to your settings and applicable laws.
* **Privacy:** Your personal data is processed according to Stripe's published Privacy Policy.
* **Dispute Resolution:** Disputes are typically resolved through **binding arbitration** (a private dispute process instead of court), with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts. This means you may not have the right to sue Stripe in court.
* **Termination:** Either party can terminate the agreement under certain conditions.
* **Contact:** You can find Stripe's contact information for questions about these terms.

**Clauses that may be harmful to the user:**

* **Dispute Resolution:** The requirement for **binding arbitration** might limit your ability to pursue a case in court. 
* **Class-action waivers:** This clause might prevent you from joining a group lawsuit against Stripe, which could reduce your chances of recovering damages.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STRIPE SERVICES AGREEMENT (US) (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Stripe and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update revised Connect platform-onboarding obligations, added Stripe Radar/AI-fraud-prevention provisions, refreshed dispute and chargeback handling sections, and updated indemnification and liability caps.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Stripe to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://stripe.com/legal/ssa . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://stripe.com/legal/ssa .

**Service Name:** Shopify Terms of Service

These _Shopify Terms of Service_ outline the rules and guidelines for using Shopify's products and services. The key provisions can be broken down into the following sections:

**Key Provisions:**

* **Scope**: These terms apply to the products and services provided by Shopify, as listed on the company's official terms page.
* **Content and License**: When you upload content to Shopify, the company can use it to operate, improve, or train their AI/ML systems, subject to your settings and applicable law.
* **Privacy**: The terms point to Shopify's published Privacy Policy, which explains how the company collects and processes your personal data.
* **Dispute Resolution**: Shopify requires binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) to resolve disputes, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts.
* **Termination**: Either party can terminate the agreement under certain conditions.
* **Contact**: If you have questions about these terms, you can visit Shopify's published legal contact information.

**Harmful Clauses:**

* The requirement for **binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court)** may be harmful to users, as it means they'll have to resolve disputes through a private process rather than going to court.
* The **30-day opt-out window for new accounts** may be a concern for some users, as it creates a limited time frame to opt-out of this provision.

**Important Note:**

The Terms of Service mention the use of user-submitted content to train AI/ML systems, and that this is subject to your settings and applicable law. However, no further details are provided in the document about what specific laws or settings you can use to control this.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — SHOPIFY TERMS OF SERVICE (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Shopify and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: 2024 update added Shopify Magic / AI-feature provisions, clarified that merchant store content may be used to power AI features only at the merchant's store level (not for training shared models), and revised payouts and risk-scoring sections.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Shopify to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://www.shopify.com/legal/terms .

[EXPECTED SUMMARY POINTS]

- Key change: 2024 update added Shopify Magic / AI-feature provisions, clarified that merchant store content may be used to power AI features only at the merchant's store level (not for training shared models), and revised payouts and risk-scoring sections.

- Users should review the cross-referenced Privacy Policy to understand data handling.

**Service Name:** Wikipedia (providing by the Wikimedia Foundation) Terms of Use

**Summary:**
The Terms of Service govern your relationship with Wikipedia and apply to the website and its services. These terms explain what happens to user content, privacy settings, and dispute resolution. Key points are summarized below.

**Key Provisions:**

* **Content and License:** When you contribute to Wikipedia, your work can be used to operate and improve the website, as well as train the company's AI/ML systems, in line with your settings and applicable laws.
* **Privacy:** The terms link to the Privacy Policy, which explains the types of personal data collected and how it's processed. However, no details are provided in the Terms of Service.
* **Dispute Resolution:** You must submit to binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) with class-action waivers, except for the first 30 days of new account creation. This means you can't join a group lawsuit against Wikipedia in most cases.
* **Termination:** Either party can end the agreement under conditions described in the current document.
* **Contact:** Questions about these terms should be directed to the company's published legal contact information.

**Clauses to note:**
- **Mandatory arbitration:** This provision may be considered detrimental to users, as it restricts their access to traditional legal channels (court) and group lawsuits (class-action).
- **Lack of transparency regarding data processing:** While the terms mention the Privacy Policy, no information about data processing is provided in the Terms of Service itself.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — WIKIMEDIA TERMS OF USE (Effective 2023; replaces the 2014 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2023 version differs from the 2014 version in the following ways: Effective June 7, 2023: first major rewrite since 2014. Added Universal Code of Conduct as binding, updated paid-contributions disclosure rules, modernized account-security and dispute-resolution provisions, and added explicit language covering automated tools and AI-assisted edits.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Wikipedia (Wikimedia Foundation) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use . The previous version is available at https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Terms_of_Use/9_June_2014 .

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The duration of data retention has increased from 18 months to 36 months after account deletion.
- The type of license granted for user content has changed to perpetual, irrevocable, and including the right to create derivative works for advertising.
- The class action waiver in the arbitration process has become unconditional, with no right to participate in a class action.
- The notice period for material changes to the Terms has been removed, and instead, continued use of the service is considered acceptance of the changes.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's review the key changes. 

The duration of data retention has increased from 18 months to 36 months after you delete your account. This means ChirpSocial will keep your account data for a longer period.

The type of license you grant for your user content has changed significantly. Previously, you only granted ChirpSocial a royalty-free license to display your content. Now, the license is worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, and royalty-free, which means ChirpSocial can use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from your content, including for advertising purposes.

Additionally, the arbitration process has been updated. Now, you waive the right to participate in any class action. This means you won't be able to join a group lawsuit against ChirpSocial if something goes wrong.

Moreover, the notice period for material changes to the Terms has been removed. Now, if ChirpSocial updates the Terms, it's considered that you accept the changes by continuing to use the service.

One new clause to note is: 
- ACCOUNT. By creating an account on ChirpSocial you agree to these Terms. This is a new main clause that makes your agreement to the Terms unconditional upon signing up.

1. ACCOUNT. By creating an account on ChirpSocial you agree to these Terms.
2. CONTENT LICENSE. You grant ChirpSocial a worldwide, perpetual, irrevocable, royalty-free license to use, distribute, modify, and create derivative works from content you post, including for advertising.
3. DATA RETENTION. We retain account data for 36 months after account deletion.
4. ARBITRATION. Disputes are resolved by binding arbitration. You waive the right to participate in any class action.
5. CHANGES. We may modify these Terms at any time. Continued use constitutes acceptance.

- The time frame for sales being final has been reduced from 14 days to 7 days after delivery.
- Returned items are now eligible for store credit only, whereas previously they were eligible for a full refund.
- Users outside the EU do not have restrictions on opting out of purchase history sharing.
- ShopFast Pay has been added as a new payment method.

[NARRATIVE]
This version adds a new payment method: ShopFast Pay, in addition to Visa, MasterCard, PayPal. 

The time frame for sales being final has changed: previously, all sales were final 14 days after delivery, while this version states they are final 7 days after delivery.

Returned items can now only be exchanged for store credit, whereas previously you were eligible for a full refund.

Opting out of purchase history sharing is still available, but it's restricted to users in the EU. Outside the EU, the opt-out option is also available, just like before.

However, there aren't any clauses that would specifically harm you; all the changes seem to impact your return and refund options as well as payment options.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Google may now use uploaded content for AI development and improvement, beyond just hosting and displaying it.
- Users are prohibited from abusing, reverse-engineering, or extracting underlying models from Google's generative-AI features.
- Arbitration requirements have been updated, but specifics are not provided in the changes.
- Liability language has been updated, but no concrete changes in the extent of liability are indicated.
- The content retention period explicitly defined as no change, as both versions do not mention it; however, prior provisions that may have defined retention periods have been reorganized.
- Dispute-governing law now seems to only remain in California, but arbitration now does not seem exclusive to regions stated in the old disputation statement.
- Warranty-disclaimers have also undergone update.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and we'll go through the changes. Let's break it down.

The biggest change is in the Content section. Previously, you granted Google a license to host, reproduce, and display your content to operate the services. Now, the license is broader, and Google may use your uploaded content to operate, develop, and **improve its services, including its AI services**. This means Google can use your content in more ways than before.

Another significant change is in the AI section. Previously, there were no specific provisions for generative AI. The new version introduces a new clause that prohibits users from:

* Abusing Google's generative-AI features
* Reverse-engineering Google's generative-AI features
* Attempting to extract underlying models from Google's generative-AI features

These are new restrictions that didn't exist in the previous version. You should be aware that attempting to reverse-engineer or extract models from Google's generative-AI features could be potentially harmful or prohibited.

The Disputes and Liability sections have also been updated, but no concrete changes are mentioned in the updated terms. It appears that arbitration requirements have been updated, but specifics are not provided.

One new thing to note is that the previous version of the content retention period didn't specify a retention period, nor did the current version. However, **prior provisions that may have defined retention periods have been reorganized**.

Lastly, the warranty disclaimers and governing law have been updated as well. The arbitration requirements and governing law are now more nuanced, but the details are not explicitly outlined.

Overall, the update broadens Google's license to use your content and adds restrictions on using Google's generative-AI features. If you have any further questions or concerns, please let me know.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The effective date of the Terms of Service changed from 2023 to 2024.
- The moderation rules are now accompanied by a link to an external Microsoft policy page.
- Third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles are allowed to track and share user data.
- Family-settings features may not be available on third-party platforms.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'll highlight the key changes for you. 

One significant change is the effective date, which has been updated to 2024. This indicates that any previous Terms of Service published in 2023 are no longer applicable.

Regarding moderation rules, the update now provides a link to an external Microsoft policy page describing moderation and enforcement in detail. This will give you a more comprehensive understanding of Microsoft's moderation policies.

Another change is related to XBOX. You should note that third-party platforms hosting Xbox titles may track and share user data, subject to those platforms' terms. This means that Microsoft is no longer solely responsible for your data collected from Xbox content on third-party platforms.

Additionally, there's a clarification on family-settings features. These features may not be available on third-party platforms, which means you won't be able to use them when accessing Xbox content on those platforms.

Considering the changes:

* The new effective date in 2024 is not likely to cause any harm.
* An external link to the moderation policy page doesn't inherently cause any harm but may require you to read and comply with more detailed rules.
* Third-party platforms tracking and sharing your data could potentially harm your confidentiality. It's essential to review and familiarize yourself with the new terms.
* Limited family-settings features on third-party platforms might affect your experience with family-related settings on Xbox.

Before using our services, I would advise you to review the changes closely, especially regarding data sharing on third-party platforms.

- The service is no longer covered by a single document, but split into Consumer Terms of Use and separate Business Terms.
- Disputes are now handled by National Arbitration and Mediation instead of ADR Services.
- The batch arbitration procedures have been revised to align with the new arbitration provider.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go over the changes.

First, the single Terms of Service document has been split into two separate documents: one for consumers and another for businesses using the API and Enterprise. This is to provide clearer boundaries and expectations for each group.

In terms of dispute resolution, the Terms of Service have changed the arbitration provider from ADR Services to National Arbitration and Mediation. This is a different organization that will handle disputes now. 

Lastly, the batch arbitration procedures have been revised to reflect how National Arbitration and Mediation handles these situations.

I don't see any new clauses that directly harm consumers, but it's essential to understand the implications of these changes. For instance, switching arbitration providers might affect the availability of resources or the overall dispute resolution process. However, I would need more context to assess potential harm.

Notable changes:

* **Split Terms of Service:** The document is now split into two separate sections: one for consumers and one for businesses.
* **Arbitration provider change:** Disputes are now handled by National Arbitration and Mediation instead of ADR Services.
* **Batch arbitration revisions:** New procedures in line with the new arbitration provider.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The Services Agreement now covers all business services under a single document, including API, ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Team, and other services. (OLD: separate per-product agreements)
- Business/API customer data is no longer used to train OpenAI's models by default. (OLD: data-handling provisions varied)
- The new agreement has consolidated and updated service-level commitments (SLAs). (OLD: commitments scattered across separate addenda)

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes to make them more unified and comprehensive. Let's walk through the key updates:

* Previously, there were separate agreements for each service (API, ChatGPT Enterprise, ChatGPT Team, etc.), but now there's a single unified Services Agreement covering all business services. This simplifies the terms and makes it easier to understand what's covered.
* One notable change is that business/customer API data is no longer used to train OpenAI's models by default. This means that your sensitive information won't be used for training purposes without your consent.
* Two other significant updates are related to indemnification and service-level agreements (SLAs). The indemnification language has been updated and consolidated, and SLAs have been updated and moved into the main agreement. This should make it clearer what's expected from both sides in terms of service commitments.

As for potential harm, I want to note that the new Terms of Service don't explicitly mention any new clauses that could directly harm you. However, it's always a good idea to review the updated agreement carefully to ensure you understand the changes and any potential implications.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The old version of the SCOPE clause was more general, while the new version is more specific with detailed product references.
- The TRAINING clause has changed from limited to explicit language, stating that customer prompts and completions are not used to train Anthropic models by default.
- The INDEMNIFICATION clause has been updated to include language tied to the published Usage Policy and is no longer mutual.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'll guide you through the changes.

**Changes to the Scope Clause**
The SCOPE clause has become more specific. In the previous version, it covered API access generally, whereas the new version has more detailed product references. The updated SCOPE clause now provides more clarity on the scope of the API access.

* **Previous clause:** Covers API access generally
* **Current clause:** Covers API access with more detailed product references

While the change doesn't introduce any negative aspects, it's good to know that the scope is better defined.

**Training Clause Update**
The TRAINING clause has undergone significant changes. The new version explicitly states that customer prompts and completions are not used to train Anthropic models by default. This is a change from the previous, more limited language that didn't explicitly address training.

* **Previous clause:** Limited explicit language about training on customer data
* **Current clause:** Explicit clause: customer prompts and completions are not used to train Anthropic models by default

This change seems to be a positive update, as it clarifies the default use case for customer data.

**Indemnification Clause Update**
The INDEMNIFICATION clause has been updated to tie in with the published Usage Policy. This change removes the mutual indemnity provision of the previous clause.

* **Previous clause:** Standard mutual indemnities
* **Current clause:** Updated indemnification and acceptable-use language tied to the published Usage Policy
* **Effect of change:** Mutual indemnity is no longer applicable; you'll need to review the Usage Policy.

The change in the indemnification clause may introduce new risks for you, as the language is now tied to the published Usage Policy. I recommend reviewing this policy to understand your obligations and potential liabilities.

**Other Changes**
Let me know if you'd like a full analysis of the remaining changes in the CUSTOMER DATA and TRAINING clauses. The new TRAINING clause will be covered in that expanded review.

To summarize, the major changes include:

* The SCOPE clause became more specific
* The TRAINING clause explicitly states customer data isn't used to train Anthropic models by default
* The INDEMNIFICATION clause changed to tie in with the published Usage Policy, which may introduce new risks

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The opening paragraph is now considered an agreement to the Terms whenever Meta products are used.
- Meta's content license is strengthened to cover use, distribution, modification of user content, in addition to display.
- Meta is now explicitly allowed to use AI and machine-learning systems on user content for service improvement and safety.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go through the changes:

The opening paragraph is now considered an agreement to the Terms whenever Meta products are used. This means simply using Meta's products (like Facebook) is enough to agree to the Terms, whereas before the Terms were mentioned explicitly. 

Meta's content license is strengthened in a few ways:
- Before, the license allowed displaying user content worldwide. 
- Now, Meta can use, distribute, and modify user content to operate and improve its services. This could potentially be a more significant impact on users, as their content might be changed in ways they can't predict.

Meta is now explicitly allowed to use AI and machine-learning systems on user content for service improvement and safety. This expands on the use of automated systems mentioned before.

One new potential point of concern is the strengthened license covering use, distribution, and modification of user content. This could, in theory, result in unforeseen changes to user-uploaded content, though the Terms of Service do not clarify the extent to which users will be notified about changes made to their content.

However, it's worth noting that the Terms of Service do not address the specifics of how user content will be used, distributed, or modified by Meta's AI and machine-learning systems.

In the previous version, the term "CROSS-PRODUCT" was mentioned, but now it's more explicit about the range of Meta Products involved, including Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and Messenger. This change seems to clarify the company's data practices.

You might want to take note of the "CONTENT LICENSE" clause, which now covers more than just hosting and displaying your uploaded content. It extends to use, distribution, and modification, which might be a concern for some users.

The "AI" clause is a new addition. It allows Meta to use AI and Machine Learning (ML) processing of your content across their products to operate and improve services. This could have implications for how your data is used and processed.

Here are some specific changes you may want to consider:

* Content License:

* AI:
 * Before: no specific clause mentioned
 * Now: allows AI/ML processing across Meta products
* CROSS-PRODUCT:
 * Before: limited references to data flowing across Meta products
 * Now: broader range of Meta products involved (Facebook, Instagram, Threads, and Messenger)

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The contracting party has been changed from TikTok Inc. to TikTok USDS.
- The content license has been reaffirmed to be irrevocable, and now explicitly includes the use for Multi-Layer (ML) model development.
- The AI section now includes new rules for generative-AI, specifically stating that AI outputs are provided 'as is' and users are responsible for their inputs and outputs.
- It is no longer allowed for users to remove watermarks or claim AI-generated output is human-made.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's break down the changes. 

The contracting party has been changed from TikTok Inc. to TikTok USDS. This simply means the entity responsible for enforcing these Terms of Service has been updated.

The most significant change is to the content license. Previously, it was a worldwide royalty-free sublicensable license. Now, it has been reaffirmed as such, and it explicitly includes the use of user content for Multi-Layer (ML) model development. This means TikTok or third parties may use and develop models using your content without any monetary compensation to you or any obligation to credit your work.

Regarding access and use by children, the Terms of Service have reaffirmed the rule that users under 13 must use the Under-13 Experience.

Lastly, the Terms of Service have added new rules for AI. Specifically:

* AI outputs are provided 'as is', implying that TikTok may not guarantee the quality or characteristics of AI-generated content.
* You are responsible for the inputs and outputs of the AI. If AI misinterprets or misuses your input, that's your responsibility, not TikTok's.
* You may not remove or strip watermarks from AI-generated content.
* You may not claim that AI-generated content is human-made.

These new AI rules can be seen as limiting user control over their interactions with AI tools on TikTok.

4. AI. New generative-AI rules: outputs are 'as is'; users are responsible for inputs/outputs; users may not strip watermarks or claim AI output is human-made.

* The term "TAX" introduces new U.S. tax-withholding obligations for non-U.S. creators receiving payments. This may affect creators outside the U.S. who earn money from their YouTube channels.

- Collection of facial-recognition data from videos (new restriction)

- Adobe can access user content for service purposes via manual methods (previously all methods were allowed, including automated). 
- Adobe will no longer train generative-AI models on customer cloud content.
- Language used in the Terms will be clearer and more easy to understand.
- Users are now provided with plain-English summaries of changes to the Terms.

[NARRATIVE]
The updated Terms of Service introduce several changes. Most notably, Adobe is now only allowed to access user content through manual methods, whereas previously, Automated methods were also permitted. This change is reflected in the wording around "service purposes."

One significant change is the clarification on Adobe's use of artificial intelligence (AI). Initially, the Terms did not adequately address this issue. However, after public backlash, it was explicitly stated that Adobe does not train generative-AI models on customer cloud content. This is a positive development for users.

Additionally, the Terms have been rewritten in clearer, plain language, making them easier to understand. Adobe also added plain-English summaries of changes alongside the Terms, which should help users stay informed about revisions.

Upon reviewing the changes, I didn't identify any new clauses that explicitly harm users. The updates focus on clarifying and improving the user experience, not introducing new restrictions.

Here are the key changes highlighted in bullets:
* Adobe can access user content for service purposes via manual methods (previously all methods were allowed, including automated).
* Adobe will no longer train generative-AI models on customer cloud content.
* Language used in the Terms will be clearer and more easy to understand.
* Users are now provided with plain-English summaries of changes to the Terms.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Zoom now has a broad license to use service-generated data (previously limited) to train AI/ML models as of March 2023.
- Zoom will only use customer audio/video/chat for AI model training with explicit customer consent (was not explicitly stated before).
- There is no change to customer-controlled use of customer content.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone changes, mainly focusing on how Zoom uses your data. 

Firstly, regarding **Service-Generated Data**, the Terms of Service previously addressed how Zoom uses *telemetry and operational data*, but this has changed. As of the March 2023 update, Zoom acquired a broader license to use **Service-Generated Data**. This now includes using it to train AI/ML models.

However, there is a crucial point regarding **AI TRAINING**. Prior to the August 2023 update, there was no specific mention of AI model training. But, to address customer concerns, the Terms of Service now require **express consent** from customers before Zoom uses their audio, video, or chat content to train AI models. 

**Customer Content** remains under customer control, which is a positive point. On the other hand, the change in how Zoom uses Service-Generated Data for AI training may have implications, though these may be outweighed by the transparency introduced around customer consent.

Overall, the most notable change is the updated clause on AI model training, ensuring customer consent is a prerequisite.
source_tos:
1. SERVICE-GENERATED DATA. March 2023 update added a broad license over Service-Generated Data permitting Zoom to use it to train AI/ML models.
2. AI TRAINING. After backlash in August 2023, Zoom amended the Terms to expressly state that audio, video, and chat content are not used to train AI models without customer consent.
3. CUSTOMER CONTENT. Customer audio/video/chat continues to be subject to customer-controlled use.

The Terms of Service have been updated. Let's review what's new.

**New Clause: AI TRAINING**

The Terms of Service now explicitly allow LinkedIn to use member data and content to train generative-AI models for LinkedIn features (`1. CONTENT LICENSE: Same baseline license, with explicit reference to use for AI training`) and even provide an opt-out toggle in Settings (`3. SETTINGS: New opt-out toggle in Settings for AI training`).

However, if you don't opt out, you're agreeing to let LinkedIn use your data and content for AI training.

**Changes to DISPUTES**

The dispute-resolution provisions have been updated (`4. DISPUTES: Updated dispute-resolution provisions, including class-action waiver language`). This includes language that potentially limits your ability to file a class-action lawsuit against LinkedIn.

**Opt-out for AI Training**

It's good to know that you can opt out of having your data and content used for AI training (`3. SETTINGS: New opt-out toggle in Settings for AI training`). Just go to the Settings and check if there is an AI training opt-out toggle.

There isn't a clause in the new Terms of Service that I can highlight as particularly problematic. However, always be cautious when accepting changes to service agreements, and make sure you understand what changes you're agreeing to.

- Explicit permission is now needed to use Slack data to train large language models, a restriction not present in the old version.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's take a look at the changes. 

The main changes are related to how apps interact with your data on Slack. Here's what's new:

* **Bulk Extraction**: We've made the rules stricter for bulk extraction by apps. Now they need to follow specific rules to do this.
* **Data-export limits**: We've clarified the limits for how much data apps can export. This means there are clearer guidelines for what they can and can't do.
* **Large Language Models (LLMs)**: Now, apps need your explicit permission to use your Slack data to train large language models. This wasn't a specific rule before, so it's a new addition.

These changes are aimed at giving you more control over your data and ensuring it's used responsibly.

As for any potential harm, the new rules are mainly restrictive on apps that might access, export, or use your data without permission. However, the Terms of Service do not address any direct harm to you. 

If you're concerned about how these changes might affect you or your apps, it's best to review these rules and decide accordingly.

- Personal data may now be shared with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates.
- Personal data may be used for AI/ML model development and training.
- The use of personal data for AI/ML model development, improvement, and training is now explicitly allowed.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes. I'll break down what's new and highlight any significant changes.

**Changes to Data Sharing:**
The Terms of Service now explicitly state that GitHub will share personal data with Microsoft and other GitHub affiliates for **AI/ML model development**. This is a new reason for sharing personal data, which wasn't mentioned in the previous version. 

**New Processing Purposes:**
There's a new purpose for processing personal data, specifically for **product development**, including **AI/ML model training**. This means that GitHub can use personal data to train and improve its AI/ML models.

**Updated Opt-Outs:**
User opt-out preferences and enterprise data protections now travel with the data when it's shared with GitHub affiliates. This means that if you've opted out of data sharing, your preferences will be respected even when the data is shared with affiliates.

**Other Changes:**
The previous version of the Terms of Service only allowed personal data sharing with affiliates for **limited operational purposes**. Now, it can be shared for AI/ML model development, improvement, and training. 

In particular, the updated clause highlights a change in how personal data will be used and shared.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The license grant for user content now explicitly allows Reddit to license user content to third parties, including for AI training.
- The terms now allow Reddit to license user content for AI training purposes.
- New provisions have been added to govern monetization-related activities.
- The dispute resolution venue has been changed.

[NARRATIVE]
Let's go over what's new. The update affects how Reddit can use your content. Previously, when you posted on Reddit, you granted them a license to use your content for their own purposes. Now, that license extends to permit Reddit to license your content to _third parties_ (including for _AI training_). This means they can share or use your content with outside companies or for AI development purposes.

Here are some key highlights from the update:

* **License grant extended**: Reddit now has rights to license your content to others, like third-party companies or AI developers.
* **AI training included**: Your content can be used to train AI systems, which might worry some users concerned about AI-generated content or potential misuse.
* **New monetization rules**: The update adds new guidelines on how Reddit handles money-making activities related to user content.
* **Dispute resolution shifted**: The process for resolving disputes, like claims about user content, has been changed.

Based on these updates, the license grant has broadened significantly, and you might want to be cautious if you're sensitive about how your content is used.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The company now includes AI processing of user-uploaded content in the standard license.
- Rules have been added for using AI to generate DJ mixes and playlists.
- The dispute resolution arbitration and class-action waiver clauses have been updated.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service say the user-uploaded content license has been expanded. Previously, it only applied to podcasts, but now it covers AI processing of uploaded audio and podcasts, as well. What this means is that when you upload content to Spotify, you're giving us permission to use it in ways we hadn't covered before, like using AI to transform or create new content from your uploaded audio.

This version adds rules for using AI to generate DJ mixes and playlists. Specifically, these rules cover AI DJ and AI-generated playlists. We don't mention what specifically is allowed or disallowed under these new rules, so we can only speculate.

Regarding disputes, there have been some changes. Arbitration is a private dispute process instead of court (binding arbitration), and you waiving your right to join a class-action lawsuit. This means if you have an issue with Spotify, you'll settle it privately with the company, rather than taking part in a group lawsuit with others.

As for new clauses that may harm you, the Terms of Service do not specifically outline any risks you should be aware of regarding AI processing or AI-generated content from your uploaded audio. However, please note that you are giving Spotify these new permissions, so you may not have any control over how they use your content once you've uploaded it.

That being said, the Terms of Service don't mention any new clauses that explicitly harm users. If you have specific concerns, I recommend reviewing the updated Terms and reaching out directly to Spotify for clarification.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- The primary Netflix household no longer includes users outside of it.
- Additional members outside the primary household must be paid for.
- The term 'Netflix Household' is now defined.
- The billing/cancellation provisions have been updated to reflect the extra-member fee.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes, mostly related to how Paid Sharing works and the billing process.

Previously, account sharing across households was generally tolerated (although it wasn't explicitly allowed). However, this version introduces a 'Netflix Household' concept, which clearly defines what is considered part of the primary household.

Here's a summary of the key changes:

* **Paid Sharing**: No longer does the primary household include users outside of it. **You may now need to pay extra for users outside of your household**.
* **HOUSEHOLD**: A defined 'Netflix Household' is now specified, clarifying what is included in the primary household.
* **BILLING**: The billing and cancellation provisions have been updated to reflect the extra-member fee, which may affect your **monthly costs if you have multiple members outside your household**.

One new concept that may impact you is the defined 'Netflix Household'. This is now a key term, which previously wasn't explicitly stated. Understand that the primary household no longer includes users outside of it, and you may need to pay extra for each additional member. 

If you have multiple family members or friends outside of your household, you should review the updated Terms of Service to ensure you understand the new requirements and any additional costs involved.

1. SHARING. Paid sharing requires the primary household plus paid additional members for users outside it.
2. HOUSEHOLD. Adds a defined 'Netflix Household' concept.
3. BILLING. Updated billing/cancellation provisions to reflect the extra-member fee.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- ADS: Subscribers on 'no ads'/'ad-free' tiers may see ads in their streaming titles.
- ADS: 'No ads'/'ad-free' tiers are no longer genuinely ad-free.
- ARBITRATION: Arbitration procedures now include expanded mass-arbitration procedures.
- EFFECTIVE DATE: New and existing subscribers will have different effective dates.

[NARRATIVE]
With the updated Terms of Service, there have been some significant changes. Let's dive into the details.

**Advertising (ADS)**: Unfortunately, the new Terms of Service say that even subscribers on the 'no ads' or 'ad-free' tiers may see ads in their streaming titles. This is a change from the previous version, where these tiers were genuinely ad-free.

**Arbitration**: The Terms of Service have been updated to include expanded mass-arbitration procedures. This means that arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) will now cover more cases, including potentially wrong cases. This change was made in response to backlash from a wrongful-death case.

**Effective Date**: Another change affects the Effective Date clause. Now, new and existing subscribers will have different effective dates. This means that if you signed up before the change, your Terms of Service will be different from those that apply to new subscribers.
source_tos:
1. ADS. Streaming titles may include ads even for subscribers on 'no ads' / 'ad-free' tiers.
2. ARBITRATION. Expanded mass-arbitration procedures (response to wrongful-death case backlash).
3. EFFECTIVE DATE. Different effective dates for new and existing subscribers.
previous_tos:
1. ADS. 'No ads' / 'ad-free' tiers were genuinely ad-free for streaming titles.
2. ARBITRATION. Standard arbitration provisions.
3. EFFECTIVE DATE. Single effective date for all subscribers.
ground_truth:

- Ads may now appear on previously ad-free / 'no ads' tiers.

- Staggered effective dates for new vs. existing subscribers.

- Subscription model and base price tiers remain similar in structure.

substantial

- The document now addresses AI-generated outputs and their interaction with the user agreement.
- Small claims court cases are no longer subject to mandatory binding arbitration.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have indeed been updated. 

The scope of the Terms of Service now encompasses Alexa and Rufus AI, as well as other AI services (1). This broader scope is intended to apply to all interactions with these services.

One notable change is the introduction of new references to AI-generated outputs. The Terms of Service now explicitly address how these outputs interact with your agreement, but the specifics of what this means and how it affects you are not outlined in the updated clauses.

Another important change is the addition of small-claims-court carve-out from arbitration (ARBITRATION clause). Previously, all disputes were subject to mandatory binding arbitration. However, with the updated Terms of Service, you may still opt to resolve disputes through small-claims courts instead of arbitration.

It's worth noting that the updated Terms of Service do not explicitly mention any new clauses that might harm you. However, the lack of clarity surrounding AI-generated outputs and their interaction with your agreement could potentially raise issues.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The OLD version allowed for standard encryption-at-rest, but the NEW version adds an optional feature for end-to-end encryption for additional iCloud data categories
- In the NEW version, Apple's access to stored content for legal/safety reasons is narrowed, implying more stringent limitations, where end-to-end encryption applies
- The NEW version introduces Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute, a server-side AI technology, which suggests new levels of data processing, in addition to its absence in the OLD version

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and here's what changed:

Apple has added an **Advanced Data Protection** feature, which allows you to opt-in for end-to-end encryption on additional iCloud data categories. This means that your data will be encrypted in a way that only you can access it. This is a new option, and you can choose to enable it if you want to.

On the other hand, when it comes to Apple's access to your data, the Terms of Service now clarify and narrow when Apple can access your stored content. In the past, Apple could access your data for legal or safety reasons, but now the Terms state that Apple will only access your data in those situations where end-to-end encryption doesn't apply.

Additionally, the updated Terms of Service introduce **Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute**, a server-side AI technology. This means that Apple will be processing your data on their servers using AI, and this processing will be done in a way that preserves your privacy.

In terms of potential harm, I want to note that the new Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute clause suggests that Apple will be processing your data on their servers using AI, which might raise concerns about data collection and processing. However, the Terms of Service state that this processing will be done in a way that preserves your privacy.

Here are the key changes in bullet points:

* Added **Advanced Data Protection** feature with optional end-to-end encryption for additional iCloud data categories.
* Narrowed access to your stored content for Apple, where end-to-end encryption applies.
* Introduced **Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute**, a server-side AI technology for data processing, with a focus on preserving your privacy.

It's essential to understand that these changes are now a part of the updated Terms of Service, and they might have an impact on how Apple handles your data. I recommend taking a closer look at the new features and understanding their implications.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The crowd-sourced services are now explicitly named as Live and Local.
- The pre-arbitration procedure now includes a 60-day waiting period that did not exist previously.
- A new section on generative-AI features (My AI and other) has been added.
- The user content license has been expanded for Live, Local, and other crowd-sourced services.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes. Let's break down what's new.

* The user-content license has been expanded for Live and Local services, which are explicitly mentioned as crowd-sourced services. This means you're granting these services a broader license to use your content.
* The new section on generative-AI features, including My AI, has been added. This section isn't flagged as concerning, but we'll have to wait and see how it's implemented.
* The arbitration procedure now includes a 60-day waiting period before proceeding to arbitration. This is a longer waiting period than before, but it might be to your benefit if you have time to resolve the issue.

Regarding new clauses that may harm you: 

* The expanded user-content license for Live and Local services could potentially limit your original rights and control over your content in these services.
* The generative-AI features may generate content in your name, which raises questions about ownership and authorship.

However, it's essential to note that these are just concerns, and actual harm depends on the implementation and specific circumstances.

response:
[DELTA BULLETS]
- Customer data is no longer used to train third-party AI models without consent.
- Third-party AI models' training data usage requires explicit customer consent.
- Dropbox Dash and AI search/summary features are added, utilizing customer data.
- Original wording around AI features raised concerns about training on customer data, leading to revision.

[NARRATIVE]
This version adds new AI-powered features to Dropbox, specifically Dropbox Dash and AI search/summary features. These new features operate on customer data.

There are changes in how Dropbox will handle customer data, specifically with regards to artificial intelligence (AI) training. The Terms of Service originally didn't address how customer data might be used to train AI models, leading to concerns. Now, it explicitly states that customer data will not be used to train third-party AI models without your consent.

Another issue is that the new AI features now use customer data. Previously, the policy didn't include any information about AI training or features that work in this way.

* New clauses that might be of concern to you:
	* The use of customer data with Dropbox Dash and AI search/summary features.
	* The possibility of your data being used to train third-party AI models without your consent, although the Terms of Service now explicitly state this must have your consent.

The Terms of Service say that Dropbox will only use your data without consent to improve or develop new features (like the ones specifically mentioned), or to operate the services. However, these changes have given you more control over how your data is used for AI purposes, by introducing explicit consent as a requirement.

It's worth noting that you are still agreeing to allow Dropbox to use AI on your data, even if only for new features.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- Users now directly own outputs from Canva's generative-AI tools, with some rights reserved by Canva.
- There are new restrictions on using Canva-generated content to train other AI models in the Magic Studio.
- AI-generated content must adhere to new content-moderation and labeling requirements.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been modified. Let's review the updates. 

Firstly, when it comes to the ownership of content created using Canva's generative-AI tools, users now directly own the outputs, subject to certain rights reserved by Canva. This means users have more control over their generated content.

However, for Magic Studio users, there are new restrictions on using Canva-generated content to train other AI models. This new clause adds an additional limitation on how Magic Studio users can utilize the generated content.

In terms of moderation, AI-generated content is now subject to stricter content-moderation and labeling requirements. 

Regarding what may potentially harm you, consider this: the new clause restricting the use of Canva-generated content in AI model training could impact your ability to use the output for other purposes.

It is worth noting that these changes likely arose from updates to Canva's software capabilities or to improve user experience.

If you have specific concerns about potential harm, please provide more context so I can help.

- Standard design-ownership concept existed before (now explicitly extended to AI outputs).

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The subprocessor list has been updated.
- The terms around AI usage have been expanded to include provisions for input/output ownership and the non-training of foundational models on customer data by default.
- Enterprise plan customers can now opt for data-residency options.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have undergone some changes. Here's a summary of what's new:

**Data Protection:**

The updated Terms of Service include an **expanded list of subprocessors**, which are third-party services that handle your data on behalf of Notion. While the Terms don't explicitly state what this means for your data, it's a good idea to review the updated list to ensure it aligns with your expectations.

**Notion AI:**

This version adds provisions for **Notion AI**, which includes terms on:
* **Input/Output Ownership**: If you use Notion AI, you maintain ownership of the input data provided, as well as any generated output.
* **No Training of Foundational Models on Customer Data (by default)**: Notion doesn't train its foundational models on customer data (e.g., your notes, projects) by default. However, this doesn't preclude all training on customer data; it's "by default."

**Enterprise Plans:**

The updated Terms introduce **data-residency options for Enterprise plans**. This change might appeal to businesses that require more control over where their data is stored. Data residency allows you to choose the specific region where your data will be hosted.

As for any potential harm, the new Terms don't explicitly mention any negative changes. However, it's always a good idea to review the updated subprocessor list to ensure it meets your standards.

Keep in mind that if you have specific concerns or questions about the changes, you should consult the updated Terms of Service for the most accurate and up-to-date information.

- Clarified that customer file content is used to train third-party generative models only with opt-in (previously non-specified).
- Strengthened language regarding security and incident notification (new version is more rigorous).

The updated Terms of Service include several changes.

First, let's talk about AI features. The new Terms of Service mention the addition of Figma AI features, including Make Designs and Visual Search. This is a new addition, and the Terms of Service don't specify any specific implications for users.

Moving on to customer files: the main change here is that customer file content is now protected, and Figma will not use this content to train third-party generative models without prior opt-in from the user. This is an improvement over the previous Terms of Service, which didn't specify this limitation.

Finally, the updated Terms of Service have strengthened the security and incident-notification language. However, the new language doesn't appear to introduce any specific risks or liabilities for users.

As for new clauses that may harm you, the only change that might have an impact is the opt-in requirement for using customer file content to train third-party generative models. To avoid your file content being used for this purpose, you should clearly opt-out or not enable these features when they are available.

Here are some key takeaways:

* Figma AI features have been added.
* Your custom file content will not be used to train third-party generative models without your explicit opt-in.
* Security and incident-notification language has been strengthened in the new Terms of Service.

[DELTA BULLETS]
- The notice window for disputes was extended to a longer period in the OLD version, but shortened in the NEW version.
- Class-action rights were not waived in the OLD version, but are now limited in the NEW version.
- Arbitration was previously governed by general legal procedures, but is now mandatory in the NEW version.
- Consumers can opt-out of the new arbitration terms within 30 days, as opposed to no such provision in the OLD version.
- The effective date of the update changed from a pre-"data-breach version" to shortly after the October 2023 data breach.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated with several changes. 

One of the key changes is related to arbitration. Previously, disputes were governed by general legal procedures; now they are mandatory and governed by a binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court). This new clause is likely to change the outcome of disputes in your favor, but it's a significant change nonetheless.

Another notable change affects class-action rights. In the previous version, class actions were not waived; now they are limited. This may limit your ability to join a larger group of users to file a lawsuit against us.

The notice window for disputes has also changed. In the previous version, it was longer; now it's been shortened. This means you'll have less time to respond to a dispute, which could be seen as a drawback.

Finally, the effective date of the update has shifted to shortly after the October 2023 data breach. This change does not inherently impact you, but it suggests a connection between the terms update and the breach.

Additionally, a new clause titled OPT-OUT is added: you now have the opportunity to opt out of the new arbitration terms within 30 days. However, if you choose to opt-out, you'll be subject to the previous arbitration terms, which do not have the same benefits as the mandatory arbitration.

In terms of clauses that may harm you, the shortened notice window, limited class-action rights, and mandatory arbitration may be seen as drawbacks. Always review our policies carefully to ensure you understand your rights and obligations.

The updated Terms of Service appear to have removed some mandatory-requirements, giving you more options for resolving disputes.

[NARRATIVE]
The Terms of Service have been updated, and I'd be happy to walk you through what changed.

The first change is to Epic Accounts. The language has been revised. While the specific changes aren't detailed in the update, it's likely a general tweaking of the language surrounding your account, such as the terms of your Epic Games account and the information Epic can collect about you.

Another change pertains to User-Generated Content (UGC). Previously, the Terms of Service only mentioned "Limited creator-payout language." Now, there are "New User-Generated Content (UEFN) provisions and creator-payout rules." This indicates a more comprehensive approach to handling user-generated content, which may provide more clarity or possibly stricter rules on how UGC is handled.

A change affecting users in the European Union (EU) is the updated language regarding EU consumer rights. Previously, it referenced standard pre-DMA language. Post-DMA generally refers to laws implemented after the Distance Marketing of Consumer Financial Services Directive (DMA) for EU consumers (that is, laws meant to protect consumers when entering into business agreements such as online contracts).

Lastly, the dispute-resolution sections have been refreshed. While the new language may not be detailed, refreshing the sections usually implies an updating of the methods used to resolve disputes, possibly including more choices for binding arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court).

As for new clauses that may harm you, I would say that the only potential red flag is the introduction of "New User-Generated Content (UEFN) provisions and creator-payout rules." While it provides more clarity, stricter rules surrounding UGC could potentially result in more limitations on how you can use and share your own content.

- Arbitration now applies revised provisions after the New Jersey Uber Eats arbitration decision (previously standard arbitration provisions pre-NJ Uber Eats decision).

Let's review the changes. The Terms of Service have revised the arbitration clause after a court decision in New Jersey. This means arbitration (a private dispute process instead of court) now follows a different set of rules.

Additionally, the Terms of Service have added language about AI-generated trip summaries and driver/rider safety features under the AI section. This means you're now expected to abide by safety standards related to these AI-generated features.

Lastly, the liability limitations for third-party services have been expanded. This change affects who you can hold liable (responsible) for issues with third-party services.

One area where this new version might impact you is in **arbitration**. Previously, arbitration provisions followed standard rules, but the updated Terms now reflect the New Jersey Uber Eats decision. It's essential to review the specifics of the arbitration process, but bear in mind that arbitration can limit your ability to sue in court.

* Other than these modifications, I haven't seen any new clauses under 'THIRD-PARTY LIABILITY' or 'ARBITRATION' that would be inherently 'harm' to the user, but rather how it now is more specific in regards to third-party liability.

To clarify, let's list the key updates:

* **Changes:**
  • Arbitration now follows revised provisions after the New Jersey decision.
  • AI-generated trip summaries and driver/rider safety features have been added under the AI section.
  • Liability limitations for third-party services have been expanded.
* The updated Terms of Service do not address other significant concerns or provisions, so I recommend reviewing them carefully for other potential impacts.

Now, with the addition of AI Gateway and Workers AI specific terms, the Terms of Service provide more clarity on how these products work.

Another change is related to customer prompts and outputs in Workers AI. Previously, there was no specific carve-out for this, but now it's explicitly stated in the Terms of Service that customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI are not used to train Cloudflare models.

Lastly, the Terms of Service now have stronger rules against abuse. While the old version had standard acceptable-use rules, the new version introduces anti-scraping and AI-bot abuse rules to protect against misuse.

There are a few new clauses that might be worth noting:

* There are no explicit clauses that specifically flag potential harms, but the stronger abuse rules might prevent some malicious activities.
* However, the new rules don't necessarily protect against scenarios like:
	+ Data breaches caused by AI Gateway or Workers AI misuse
	+ Damage to your own reputation in case of AI-bot abuse
* As for AI models training, the Terms of Service now clarify that it doesn't apply to customer prompts/outputs in Workers AI specifically but does not explicitly exclude other AI products.

Keep in mind that the Terms of Service do not address every possible scenario, and it's essential to review the document carefully.

The updated Terms also address automated tools and AI-assisted edits, stating that explicit language covering these topics is now a binding policy (5. AI / AUTOMATED EDITS).

It's worth noting that the scope of the Terms hasn't changed much under the new version, however it has seen a major rewrite "since 2014 to better reflect current standards" since then, but what specifically changed in scope has not been listed out. 

There are no new clauses that flag users for potential harm that I could determine.

3. ARBITRATION. Any dispute arising from these Terms shall be resolved exclusively through binding arbitration administered by the AAA. You waive your right to a jury trial and to participate in any class action.
4. ACCOUNT TERMINATION. We may suspend or terminate your account at any time, for any reason, without prior notice.
5. CHANGES TO TERMS. We may modify these Terms at any time. Continued use after changes constitutes acceptance.
6. SUPPORT. We aim to respond to support tickets within 5 business days.

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with X (Twitter) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: Effective November 15, 2024: added an explicit, royalty-free, worldwide license for X to use posted content for training machine-learning and generative-AI models, removed the prior in-product opt-out language, and broadened third-party data-sharing permissions.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by X (Twitter) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.

user_input: Does Steam still require disputes to go to arbitration?
response: The Terms of Service say that under the 2023 version, several years of language required mandatory arbitration for disputes (a private dispute process instead of court). However, as of the 2024 update, Steam (Valve) reversed this policy. Now, they specifically require disputes to be filed in court (subject to venue rules), removing the mandatory arbitration clauses entirely.
source_tos:
SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — STEAM SUBSCRIBER AGREEMENT (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Steam (Valve) and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: September 26, 2024 update removed the mandatory arbitration / class-action waiver clauses entirely - Valve now requires disputes to be filed in court (subject to venue rules), reversing several years of arbitration-only language.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Steam (Valve) to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/ . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20230101000000*/https://store.steampowered.com/subscriber_agreement/ .

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — ANTHROPIC COMMERCIAL TERMS OF SERVICE (API) (Effective 2024; replaces the 2023 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Anthropic and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2023 version in the following ways: Added more detailed sections on customer data and outputs, clarified that customer prompts and completions are not used to train models by default, and updated indemnification and acceptable-use language tied to the published Usage Policy.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Anthropic to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/2023/https://www.anthropic.com/legal/commercial-terms .

user_input: Can I turn on end-to-end encryption for my iCloud data?
response:
The Terms of Service say that Apple now offers Advanced Data Protection, also known as end-to-end encryption, for iCloud data. This is an optional security feature that adds an extra layer of protection to your data. Note that with end-to-end encryption, even Apple won't be able to access your encrypted data, but you will still need to follow Apple's guidelines if you need assistance accessing it.  

Also, it's worth mentioning that this feature is subject to your settings and applicable law.

SUMMARY OF UPDATED TERMS OF SERVICE — ICLOUD TERMS AND CONDITIONS (Effective 2024; replaces the 2022 version)

1. SCOPE. These updated terms govern the user's relationship with Apple and apply to the products and services described on the company's official terms page.
2. WHAT CHANGED. The 2024 version differs from the 2022 version in the following ways: 2024 update added Advanced Data Protection (end-to-end encryption) language, references to Apple Intelligence Private Cloud Compute, and revised provisions about how stored content may be accessed by Apple for legal/safety reasons.
3. CONTENT AND LICENSE. The updated terms describe how user-submitted content is used by Apple to operate, improve and (where applicable) train the company's AI/ML systems, subject to the user's settings and applicable law.
4. PRIVACY. The terms cross-reference the company's published Privacy Policy, which sets out the categories of personal data collected and how it is processed.
5. DISPUTE RESOLUTION. Most updated terms in this set continue to require binding arbitration with class-action waivers, with a 30-day opt-out window for new accounts (Steam (Valve) is the notable exception in this dataset, having removed mandatory arbitration in 2024).
6. TERMINATION. Either party may terminate the agreement subject to the conditions described in the live document.
7. CONTACT. For questions about these terms, see the company's published legal contact information at the new TOS URL: https://www.apple.com/legal/internet-services/icloud/en/terms.html . The previous version is available at https://web.archive.org/web/20220101000000*/https://www.apple.com/legal/internet-services/icloud/en/terms.html .
